title: Daily Routine & Scheduling
subtitle: A day is six blocks, not forty separate jobs.
objectives: Explain the difference between a routine and a schedule
Build a day out of blocks rather than a task list
Identify fixed and flexible time in a day
Explain why a task needs a time before it gets done
Explain why a wind-down block matters

cards.title: A to-do list is a list of things you have not done
cards.text: It grows all day and never gives you permission to stop. A schedule does the opposite of both.

cards.title: Routine and schedule are not the same
cards.text: The exam asks for the difference, and it is worth having straight anyway.
points: **A routine** is a fixed order of actions. Same every time.
**A schedule** is what happens at what time.
**A routine has no clock.** A schedule does.
**You need both.** They solve different problems.

cards.title: Six blocks, tapped one at a time
cards.text: Not forty jobs. Six. Two quiz questions come from this.

question.text: What is the difference between a routine and a schedule?
options: A routine is an order of actions; a schedule attaches times
A routine is written down; a schedule is remembered
A routine is for adults; a schedule is for students
question.explain: A routine is the same order every time, with no clock. A schedule puts it on a clock.

cards.title: Start from what you cannot move
cards.text: School, meals and sleep are fixed. Building around them is much easier than building from scratch.
points: **Fixed** — school, meals, bedtime, training sessions.
**Flexible** — homework, chores, free time.
**Place the fixed ones first.**
**The gaps are your real day.** There are fewer than you think.

cards.title: Every training plan is blocks
cards.text: Warm-up, technical, rounds, conditioning, stretch. Nobody writes a list of forty exercises and hopes.
points: **Each block has a job** and a length.
**You know when it ends.** That is why you can push.
**An open-ended session** gets less work done.
**Your evening works the same way.**

question.text: Which of these is FIXED time in a school day?
question.explain: School does not move. Build the flexible things around the fixed ones, not the other way round.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Blocks are set. Part 2 is why a job needs a time, and how a day ends properly. Your place is saved.

cards.title: A task without a time is a wish
cards.text: "I'll do it later" has no time in it. Later is not a time, and that is exactly why it does not happen.

cards.title: Give every job a when
cards.text: Moving a task from a list into a block is the single change that gets it done.
points: **"Homework"** is a wish. **"Homework, 5:30"** is a plan.
**A block has an end**, which makes starting easier.
**Nothing on a list argues with anything else.**
**Things in a schedule do**, and that is useful.

cards.title: Games never give you an open-ended task
cards.text: There is always a marker, a timer or a distance. You are never told to just make progress at some point.
points: **A clear end** is what makes it possible to start.
**Progress you can see** is why you keep going.
**A block is a quest marker** for your evening.
**Copy the design.** It works on purpose.

question.text: Why does giving a task a specific time help?
options: A block has an end, which makes it easier to start
It means you can skip it if you are busy
It makes the task more important
question.explain: Later is not a time. A block that ends is much easier to begin than an open-ended job.

cards.title: The wind-down is the one people skip
cards.text: It is thirty to sixty minutes and it decides how the next morning goes. Skipping it costs tomorrow, not tonight.
points: **Screens down** before bed, not in bed.
**Bag packed. Kit out. Tomorrow decided.**
**Light and screens delay sleep** measurably.
**A bad morning usually started the night before.**

cards.title: Sleep is when you actually grow
cards.text: Growth hormone is released in the deepest stage of sleep. Training builds nothing until you sleep on it.
points: **Muscle is repaired during sleep**, not during training.
**Around nine hours** is normal at your age.
**A regular bedtime beats a long one.**
**The wind-down block protects all of it.**

question.text: A wind-down block affects the next morning more than the current evening.
question.explain: True. Kit packed, decisions made, sleep protected. A bad morning usually started the night before.

terms.def: A fixed order of actions, done the same way each time. No clock involved.
What happens at what time. A routine placed on a clock.
A named stretch of time with a start, an end and one job.
Parts of the day you cannot move: school, meals, bedtime.
The gaps you can decide about: homework, chores, free time.
The last block of the day. Screens down, kit ready, tomorrow decided.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **A routine is an order. A schedule has a clock.**
**Place the fixed things first.** Build round them.
**A task without a time is a wish.**
**The wind-down block** pays out tomorrow morning.

options: A fixed order of actions, done the same way each time
A list of times for the day
A list of jobs to finish
A plan for the whole week
quiz.explain: An order with no clock. Add times to it and you have a schedule.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between a routine and a schedule

quiz.text: What does a schedule add that a routine does not have?
quiz.explain: A routine is the same order every time. A schedule puts that order on a clock.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between a routine and a schedule

quiz.text: Which of these is FLEXIBLE time?
quiz.explain: Homework can move. School, meals and bedtime are the fixed points you build around.
quiz.objective: Identify fixed and flexible time in a day

quiz.text: When building a day, what should you place first?
quiz.explain: Fixed points first. The gaps between them are the day you actually get to decide about.
quiz.objective: Build a day out of blocks rather than a task list

quiz.text: A to-do list tells you when you are finished for the day.
quiz.explain: False. It grows all day and never gives permission to stop. A block has an end; a list does not.
quiz.objective: Build a day out of blocks rather than a task list

quiz.text: Why is "I'll do it later" a problem?
options: Later is not a time, so nothing schedules it
It means the job is unimportant
quiz.explain: A task without a when is a wish. Moving it into a block is the change that gets it done.
quiz.objective: Explain why a task needs a time before it gets done

quiz.text: Why is a block easier to start than an open-ended job?
options: It has an end you can see
quiz.explain: Knowing when it stops is what makes it possible to begin. Games use the same design.
quiz.objective: Explain why a task needs a time before it gets done

quiz.text: What belongs in a wind-down block?
options: Screens down, bag packed, kit laid out
The hardest homework of the day
quiz.explain: It is about removing tomorrow's decisions and protecting sleep, not about getting more done.
quiz.objective: Explain why a wind-down block matters

quiz.text: Growth hormone is released mainly during deep sleep.
quiz.explain: True. Training is the signal, sleep is when the building happens. Skipping sleep wastes the session.
quiz.objective: Explain why a wind-down block matters

quiz.text: Put a normal weekday evening in order.
quiz.explain: Hard physical work first makes sitting still afterwards easier. Wind-down always goes last.
quiz.objective: Build a day out of blocks rather than a task list

quiz.text: Why does free time work better when it is scheduled?
options: Unplanned free time gets eaten by everything else
It stops you enjoying it too much
quiz.explain: If it has no block, other things expand into it. Scheduling it is what protects it.
quiz.objective: Build a day out of blocks rather than a task list

quiz.text: Which is a schedule rather than a routine?
options: Always putting keys in the same bowl
quiz.explain: Times make it a schedule. The other three are orders of actions with no clock attached.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between a routine and a schedule

teacher.summary: Week 2 TLE covers daily routine and scheduling, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. It argues against the to-do list, which is the format most students are handed and the one that works least well for a learner who struggles to start: a list grows all day and never signals completion, while a block has an end. The dayBlocks figure shows a whole weekday as six blocks rather than as a task list, and the ordering in it is deliberate — training before homework, because hard physical work makes sitting still afterwards easier. The wind-down block gets its own section because it is the one that is always dropped first and the one that pays out the following morning.
discussion: Ask him to name the fixed points in his own day. Everything else is negotiable, and seeing that is the point.
Ask what 'later' actually means. Getting to 'it means no time at all' is the whole second half.
Compare a training plan to an evening. Both are blocks, and he already trusts one of them.
Ask what would have to happen for a wind-down block to survive a bad day. That is where it usually breaks.
teacher.extension: Have him draw his real Tuesday as six blocks on paper, then run it for one week and mark which blocks held. The blocks that fail tell you more than the ones that work.
misconceptions: 'A routine and a schedule are the same thing.' A routine is an order of actions. A schedule attaches times to it.
'A longer to-do list means a more productive day.' A list has no end, so it never signals that you are finished.
'Free time does not need scheduling.' Unscheduled free time gets absorbed by everything around it.
'Sleep is time lost from training.' Growth hormone is released in deep sleep. The session does nothing without it.
